title: Jeremiah 14:1–9
context: Jeremiah 14 opens with the LORD’s word to Jeremiah about a drought. A poem describes Judah, Jerusalem, nobles, farmers, and even wild animals suffering for lack of rain. Then a voice, most likely the people or Jeremiah praying on their behalf, confesses sin and pleads with the LORD, the hope of Israel, not to leave them. Both traditions read the passage as shared ground about human dependence on God and confession that appeals to his name.

verses.text: This is the LORD’s word that came to Jeremiah concerning the drought:
verses.arminianNotes:
The narrator introduces the LORD’s word to Jeremiah concerning the drought. The setting is a land without rain.

Arminian readers see God speaking into a real crisis, calling his people to understand their situation before him.
verses.reformedNotes:
The date of this drought is not given, and attempts to fix it are tentative.

Reformed readers see God’s word interpreting events in his people’s history. Both traditions read this as shared ground about God speaking through his prophet in times of distress.

verses.text: “Judah mourns, and its gates languish. They sit in black on the ground. The cry of Jerusalem goes up.
verses.arminianNotes:
Judah mourns, its gates languish, its people sit in black on the ground, and Jerusalem’s cry goes up. Grief fills the land.

Arminian readers see the whole community affected by drought and drawn into mourning.
verses.reformedNotes:
The gates, places of public life, are pictured as languishing with the people.

Reformed readers see covenant curses felt in daily life. Both traditions read this as shared ground and hear the poem with compassion for a suffering people, as the prophet himself does.

verses.text: Their nobles send their little ones to the waters. They come to the cisterns, and find no water. They return with their vessels empty. They are disappointed and confounded, and cover their heads.
verses.arminianNotes:
Nobles send servants to the cisterns, but they find no water and return with empty vessels, ashamed and covering their heads. Even the powerful are helpless.

Arminian readers see the drought humbling rich and poor alike.
verses.reformedNotes:
Covering the head is a sign of grief and shame. The image of empty cisterns may recall 2:13, where the people forsake “the spring of living waters.”

Reformed readers see human resources failing. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: Because of the ground which is cracked, because no rain has been in the land, the plowmen are disappointed. They cover their heads.
verses.arminianNotes:
Because the ground is cracked and there is no rain, the farmers are dismayed and cover their heads. Work is halted.

Arminian readers see the drought reaching every part of the community’s life and livelihood, from the city to the fields.
verses.reformedNotes:
The plowmen’s shame parallels that of the nobles in verse 3.

Reformed readers see dependence on God for rain laid bare. Both traditions read this as shared ground about human dependence on God’s provision, which the people themselves will confess in verse 22.

verses.text: Yes, the doe in the field also calves and forsakes her young, because there is no grass.
verses.arminianNotes:
Even the doe in the field gives birth and abandons her young, because there is no grass. Creation itself suffers.

Arminian readers see the drought’s effects reaching beyond human beings to the animals of the land.
verses.reformedNotes:
The image of a mother deer abandoning her fawn is meant to stir the reader’s pity at the depth of the crisis.

Reformed readers see creation sharing in the consequences of human sin. Both traditions read this as shared ground and hear the poem’s pathos.

verses.text: The wild donkeys stand on the bare heights. They pant for air like jackals. Their eyes fail, because there is no vegetation.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wild donkeys stand on bare heights, panting like jackals, their eyes failing for lack of vegetation. The poem closes with animals in distress.

Arminian readers see the extent of the suffering, which touches the wild as well as the settled land.
verses.reformedNotes:
The images move from city to field to wilderness, showing the whole land afflicted.

Reformed readers see the land mourning under judgment. Both traditions read this as shared ground and keep the poetry’s sorrow in view without drawing more from it than it says.

verses.text: Though our iniquities testify against us, work for your name’s sake, LORD; for our rebellions are many. We have sinned against you.
verses.arminianNotes:
The people, or Jeremiah on their behalf, confess that their iniquities testify against them and ask the LORD to act for his name’s sake. Confession turns to plea.

Arminian readers see genuine prayer (compare the box at Joshua 10:14).
verses.reformedNotes:
Whether these verses voice the people or the prophet speaking for them is not certain.

Reformed readers see an appeal resting on God’s name rather than human merit. Both traditions read this as shared ground about confession that appeals to God’s character.

verses.text: You hope of Israel, its Savior in the time of trouble, why should you be as a foreigner in the land, and as a wayfaring man who turns aside to stay for a night?
verses.arminianNotes:
The speaker calls the LORD the hope and Savior of Israel, and asks why he is like a stranger or a traveler staying only a night. The question is anguished.

Arminian readers see a people longing for God’s presence.
verses.reformedNotes:
The images express the people’s sense that God seems absent or uninvolved.

Reformed readers see faith addressing God by his covenant titles even in distress. Both traditions read this as shared ground about honest prayer in times when God seems far away.

verses.text: Why should you be like a scared man, as a mighty man who can’t save? Yet you, LORD, are in the middle of us, and we are called by your name. Don’t leave us.
verses.arminianNotes:
The speaker asks why the LORD seems like a frightened man or a warrior who cannot save, yet affirms that he is among them and they bear his name: “Don’t leave us.” The plea closes.

Arminian readers see trust expressed even in perplexity.
verses.reformedNotes:
The bold questions are followed by confession of God’s presence and covenant name.

Reformed readers see faith holding to God’s promises and to the name his people bear. Both traditions read this as shared ground.
